prompt: You usually referee an obstacle with a penalty loop. Today you're at a Stadion event and an athlete fails your obstacle. What is the penalty?
options: The obstacle's usual penalty loop
15 burpees
30 burpees
The penalty loop, then 15 burpees
feedback: At Stadion events the penalty for failing any obstacle is always 15 burpees, for every obstacle and every heat (rule 3.17.3).

prompt: An athlete says the rules must be different here because the race is in another country. What is right?
options: Each country publishes its own version of the rules
The Race Director decides which rules apply locally
One rulebook applies to every Spartan event worldwide
Only Elite and championship races follow the global rulebook
feedback: The Rules of Competition apply to all Spartan events and competitions globally and bind every competitor (rule 1.1.1). One aim is globally standardised competition (rule 1.2.1).

prompt: The programme groups Spartan's obstacles into five kinds of challenge. Which list is correct?
options: Climbing, carrying, crawling, jumping, and pulling and lifting
Climbing, carrying, swimming, throwing, and pushing and pulling
Running, climbing, crawling, throwing, and hanging and swinging
Carrying, crawling, swimming, jumping, and balancing
feedback: The five kinds are climbing, carrying, crawling, jumping, and pulling and lifting: for example the walls, the Bucket Carry, the Barbed Wire Crawl, the Fire Jump and the Hercules Hoist.

prompt: You're refereeing at a Beast. What minimum number of referees does Spartan's officiating procedure set for this format?
feedback: The minimum is 10 referees at a Sprint or Stadion, 15 at a Super, and 20 at a Beast or Ultra.

prompt: What is Spartan's stated mission?
options: To find the fastest obstacle racers in the world
To make every race harder than the last
To give elite athletes a professional circuit
To help people live without limits
feedback: Spartan's mission is to help people live without limits, by building strength, discipline and resilience. Its events are for every level, from first-timers to elite competitors.

prompt: You and the Race Director disagree on how a rule applies at your obstacle. Whose interpretation is final?
options: The Head Referee (the rulebook's Head Official)
The Race Director, who runs the overall event
Yours, as the referee posted at that obstacle
The timing team, who apply the penalties to results
feedback: The Head Official is the chief decision maker on all rules matters and the ultimate authority for interpreting them (rule 2.1.2). The Race Director runs the event's overall operations (rule 2.1.9).

prompt: In the rulebook, who counts as an 'official'?
options: Only referees and the Head Official, never volunteers or staff
Staff, referees and volunteers given authority by Spartan
Only paid Spartan staff, including the Race Director
Referees and the timing team, but not volunteers
feedback: Rule 2.1.3 defines an official as any Spartan representative designated to carry out event duties in a position of authority, including staff, referees and volunteers.

prompt: In an Elite heat at a Beast, Athlete A crosses the finish line first. Athlete B started later and had a faster start-to-finish time. Neither has a penalty. Who wins?
options: Athlete B: Elite heats are decided on chip time
Athlete B: the fastest course time always wins
Athlete A: Elite heats are decided on gun time
Neither, until the Head Referee decides
feedback: Outside Stadion, an Elite heat is won by whoever crosses the finish line first, regardless of when they crossed the start line, plus any time penalties (rule 3.22.1).

prompt: Which heats are decided on chip time?
options: Elite heats at every event, including Stadion
Open heats only; Age Group and Elite use gun time
Every Elite and Age Group heat at a Sprint, Super or Beast
Age Group and Open heats, and Elite heats at Stadion
feedback: Chip time, from crossing the start line to crossing the finish, decides Age Group and Open heats and Elite Stadion heats, with any time penalties added (rule 3.22.2).

prompt: An Age Group racer starts in the wrong heat. What is the consequence under the rulebook?
options: They are moved to the Open category
They are disqualified from the race
They get a time penalty added to their finish
They become ineligible for awards
feedback: Any racer who starts in an incorrect heat is ineligible for awards, including championship qualification (rule 3.9.1). Being moved to Open applies to Elite racers (rule 3.9.2).

prompt: How are Open category racers expected to complete burpee penalties?
options: On camera, for video review
With a referee counting each rep
As 15 burpees instead of 30
On Spartan honour
feedback: All Open category competitors are expected to use Spartan honour when completing burpee penalties (rule 3.23.1). Referees focus primarily on the Competitive categories (rule 3.2).

prompt: You've finished officiating the Elite and competitive waves at your obstacle. What happens next, depending on the event?
options: Clear down, or hand over to volunteers for Open waves
Stay and officiate every Open wave in full, as before
Go to the finish line to hear athletes' protests
Join the timing team to enter the penalties you saw
feedback: The referee's day ends with clearing down the course or handing over to volunteers for the Open waves. The Head Referee's briefing tells you which applies.

prompt: Pre-event training puts special emphasis on which obstacles?
options: Mandatory obstacles only
High-failure obstacles
Obstacles that are new this season
Obstacles with a water crossing
feedback: Pre-event training covers the rulebook with emphasis on high-failure obstacles, the ones athletes fail most often, plus the referee workflow, burpee standards and video at the Spear Throw.

prompt: What minimum battery life does the officiating procedure set for referee video cameras?
options: At least 1 hour
At least 2.5 hours
At least 1.5 hours
At least 4 hours
feedback: Cameras need at least 2.5 hours of battery, with backup batteries, plus adjustable 7 foot tripods and SD cards of at least 32 GB.

prompt: When does the Head Referee prepare and test the officiating equipment?
options: At check-in on race morning
Straight after the onsite briefing
On the Friday before the event
The evening after the race
feedback: The Head Referee prepares and tests the equipment on the Friday before the event, then hands it out on race day with final instructions.

prompt: You're assigned to the Rope Climb. Do you need a video camera and tripod?
options: Yes: every multiple-attempt obstacle is filmed
No: video is for the Spear Throw only
Yes, if the Rope Climb has a burpee zone
Only if it is a high-failure obstacle
feedback: Video recording at obstacles is for the Spear Throw only, so you carry a camera and tripod only if you're assigned to film it.

prompt: Which is true of the Head Referee's onsite briefing?
options: It's optional if you did the online training
It takes place after the first Elite wave
Only referees at the Spear Throw attend
It's mandatory, before you deploy
feedback: The onsite briefing is mandatory. It covers assignments, obstacle classifications, penalty loops, the burpee standard and how penalties are reported.

prompt: At the 7 foot wall, a female athlete chooses not to use the red step. What is the call?
options: A failure: she must use the female option
She must climb again using the step
A failure, but only in an Elite heat
No issue: she may choose not to use it
feedback: Female competitors may choose to forgo a female-specific step (rule 3.17.9). The failure is a male athlete using the red step (rule 4.1.1).

prompt: You see an athlete cut short your obstacle's penalty loop. Who do you report it to?
options: The timing team, directly
The Race Director, directly
The Head Referee
The Volunteer Coordinator
feedback: Referees report to the Head Referee, the rulebook's Head Official (rule 2.1.8). The Head Referee tells Timing about competitor incidents such as shortcuts.

prompt: At check-in on race morning, who can sign you in?
options: Only the Race Director, at the referee tent
Any member of the timing team at the start
The Volunteer Coordinator or the Head Referee
Another referee who is posted at your obstacle
feedback: You sign in with the Volunteer Coordinator or the Head Referee, at the Volunteer Tent or the referee tent. Make sure the Head Referee knows you're there.

prompt: What must the Head Referee confirm before the first Elite start?
options: That every penalty loop has been timed
That the Results Tent is open
That every referee is in position
That the Race Director has approved each referee's calls
feedback: Before the first Elite start, the Head Referee has to confirm that every referee is in position. That's why you make sure they know you've arrived.

prompt: At the Ape Hanger, an athlete climbs the ladder, touches an overhead bar, then steps back down to rest and start again. What is the call?
options: Fine: the attempt only starts at the second bar
They're committed: complete it or take the penalty
Fine: they may reset at any point until they ring the bell
A failure, followed by disqualification
feedback: At the Ape Hanger an athlete is committed once they touch any overhead bar, and must then complete the obstacle or the penalty (rule 4.2.2).

prompt: At the Rope Climb, an athlete climbs halfway, returns to the ground, then tries again on a different rope. What is the call?
options: Allowed: ropes may be changed back on the ground
A failure: they must stay on the rope they started on
A failure: only one attempt is allowed
Allowed only if the first rope was damaged
feedback: Rule 4.1.8 lets a competitor change ropes after returning to the ground and try again. Using more than one rope during a single attempt is the failure.

prompt: At a Super, an athlete's spear misses. They ask to move to a free lane and throw again. What do you do?
options: Allow it: athletes may change lanes at the Spear Throw
Refuse: it's a fail, so 30 burpees in the zone
Refuse, and send them on the penalty loop
Allow it if their tether tangled
feedback: The attempt starts once the spear is released forward, and lanes can only be changed before that. A miss is a fail: 30 burpees in the zone (rules 4.2.13 and 3.17.5).

prompt: A spear embeds cleanly. The athlete walks 3 metres from the lane, then the spear falls out. What is the call?
options: Pass: it was complete at 2 metres
Fail: the spear didn't stay in the target
An incomplete attempt: 30 burpees
A rethrow, as the spear stuck at first
feedback: The Spear Throw is complete once the athlete is at least 2 metres from the lane (rule 4.2.13). It's an incomplete attempt only if the spear falls before then.

prompt: At the Bucket Carry, an athlete asks if they can do burpees instead of carrying the bucket. What do you tell them?
options: Yes: they may do 30 burpees instead of the carry
Yes: they may do the penalty loop instead
Yes, if they're racing in an Open wave
No: there's no burpee option at the Bucket Carry
feedback: Rule 4.3.3 says there is no burpee option for the Bucket Carry: it must be completed. Failing a mandatory obstacle means disqualification unless the Race Director substitutes a time penalty (rule 3.17.2).

prompt: Your obstacle sits beyond a stretch of water. An athlete wants to skip the water and go straight to the penalty. Nobody has said that's acceptable. What is the call?
options: Allowed: taking the penalty replaces the attempt
Not allowed: reaching it is part of the attempt
Allowed, if they complete the penalty in full
Allowed at single-attempt obstacles only
feedback: An attempt can include entering water or difficult terrain to reach the obstacle. That can't be bypassed with a penalty unless the briefing or race staff allow it (rule 3.17.6).

prompt: An athlete fails a mandatory obstacle. Who can substitute a time penalty for disqualification?
options: You, the referee at the obstacle
The timing team
The Race Director
The Volunteer Coordinator
feedback: Failing a mandatory obstacle means disqualification, but the Race Director may substitute a time penalty depending on how serious it was (rule 3.17.2).

prompt: Two Age Group athletes in the same heat fail your obstacle. The second is struggling, so you think about a shorter loop. What is right?
options: Shorten it: loop distance can vary
Let the second athlete do burpees instead
Shorten it, then tell the Head Referee
Both do the same loop
feedback: A loop's distance can vary with terrain, but each penalty is applied consistently to everyone in the same category or heat (rule 3.17.3).

prompt: Outside Stadion, which penalty does the officiating procedure say most obstacles use?
options: A penalty loop; the Spear Throw uses burpees
Burpees; only the Spear Throw uses a penalty loop
30 burpees at every obstacle
Whatever the referee chooses on the day
feedback: The officiating procedure says most obstacles use a penalty loop and the Spear Throw uses burpees. Rule 3.17.3 lets Spartan set a loop or 30 burpees per obstacle, event, category or heat.

prompt: Who confirms each obstacle's penalty format before the event?
options: You, when you inspect the obstacle
The timing team, together with the Head Referee
The Volunteer Coordinator
The Head Referee, with the Race Director
feedback: Before the event, the Head Referee confirms each obstacle's penalty format with the Race Director, and the onsite briefing covers what applies to yours.

prompt: Between obstacles, a friend runs alongside an Elite athlete, coaching them and setting the pace. What is this?
options: Fine, as long as there's no physical contact at all
Fine between obstacles, just not at them
Pacing: not allowed. Record the number, report it
Fine: it's only information about the race
feedback: Pacing by any person is strictly prohibited (rule 3.16.1), and athletes may not accept pacing from anyone but a Spartan official (rule 3.6.1). Only being told about other athletes' progress or times isn't assistance.

prompt: Under the general rule on striking bells, may an athlete ring the bell with their head?
options: No: only the arms and hands may strike a bell
No: it counts the same as kicking the bell
Yes: any part above the chest may strike it
Only if both hands are still on the obstacle
feedback: Rule 3.17.7 allows bells to be struck with the arms, the hands or any other part of the body above the chest. Using the feet, legs or knees is the failure.

prompt: At the Spear Throw burpee zone, an athlete has lost their headband. What do you do?
options: Note their name, or say it on camera, and tell the Head Referee
Send them back to find it before they start
Let them do their burpees out of camera view
Turn their face towards the camera lens so the review can identify them
feedback: If an athlete has lost their headband, record their name or say who they are on the camera's audio, and tell the Head Referee. Never move an athlete's body or face for the camera.

prompt: Who keeps the official video footage, and for how long?
options: The referee who filmed it, until the award ceremony
The timing team, until results are final
The Race Director, for a week after the race
The Head Referee, until the end of the event day
feedback: The Head Referee manages the video review, keeps the footage until the end of the event day, and never gives it to athletes.

prompt: Under rule 3.17.4, what is the top position of a burpee?
options: Balanced and upright, with hips and knees extended
A squat with the knees bent, ready to jump
Kneeling upright with a straight back and arms up
Standing bent forward at the hips, hands on the knees
feedback: Rule 3.17.4 defines the top position as balanced and upright, with the hips and knees extended. The jump comes after it.

prompt: Mid-penalty, an athlete loses count and asks how many burpees they've done. What do you say?
options: Athletes count their own: you watch the standard
Give them your count, so they can finish correctly
Tell them to start again from zero
Tell them to stop: the video will count them
feedback: Athletes are responsible for counting their own burpees, and referees don't count for them. Your job is to watch that every rep meets the standard.

prompt: An athlete does 30 burpees to the standard, but the last 4 are outside the burpee zone. How many count towards the penalty?
options: None: they must start again
feedback: Burpees completed outside the designated zone don't count towards the penalty (rule 3.17.5), so 4 are still owed.

prompt: In the video review, what is checked about an athlete's burpees?
options: Only how many were done; quality is your job
Only whether they were in the zone
Only the last few reps
Both how many were done and how well
feedback: Under the officiating procedure, the review decides on both the number and the quality of the burpees. That's why missed and incorrect burpees are treated alike.

prompt: An athlete does very fast burpees. Every rep has the chest on the ground, full extension at the top and a jump with hands above the ears. What is your call?
options: Require extra reps: fast burpees aren't one continuous movement
They count: speed isn't a fault if the standard is met
Require extra reps: each rep must be slow
Refer it to the Head Referee before they go on
feedback: What matters is whether each rep meets rule 3.17.4 as one continuous movement. Fast reps that meet every part of the standard are complete burpees.

prompt: At the top of each rep, an athlete jumps straight from a half-squat, hips still bent. What do you do?
options: Accept them: there's a jump with hands above the ears
Accept them, as the chest touched the ground
Stop them and send them to the Head Referee
Require extra burpees: hips must be extended first
feedback: The top position needs the hips and knees extended before the jump (rule 3.17.4). A rep without it isn't complete, so require extra burpees and explain calmly why.

prompt: An athlete stands fully upright and raises their hands above their ears, but doesn't jump. Does the rep count?
options: No: a complete burpee ends with a jump
Yes: hands above the ears is what matters
Yes, as long as the chest touched the ground
Only if it's the last rep of the penalty
feedback: Rule 3.17.4 requires a jump with the hands extended above the ears after the top position. A rep with no jump isn't complete.

prompt: Where are penalties given in the official video review made available?
options: At each obstacle's burpee zone, as they are given
Only online, after the awards
At the start line, before the next wave
Inside the Results Tent, during the review
feedback: Penalties given during the official video review are made available inside the Results Tent throughout the review (rule 3.18.3).

prompt: When does the competitor protest period normally end?
options: As soon as the provisional results are posted on site
One hour after the athlete finishes
15 minutes before their category's award ceremony
When the award ceremony starts
feedback: The protest period starts as soon as the athlete crosses the finish line and ends 15 minutes before the official award ceremony for their category (rule 3.19.1).

prompt: During a dispute, an athlete pushes you. What does the rulebook say about this?
options: You may disqualify them on the spot
It can be grounds for suspension
It only counts if another official saw it
It's settled by a time penalty you set
feedback: Physical violence towards a race official is grounds for suspension (rule 3.11.1). Your part is to record the number and what happened, and report it to the Head Referee.

prompt: In the official video review, an athlete submits a spectator's photo of their attempt. Must officials consider it?
options: No: they aren't obliged to consider it
Yes: all evidence must be reviewed
Yes, if the photo is time-stamped
Only if the athlete raced in an Elite heat
feedback: Race officials aren't obliged to review or consider any video or photo taken by competitors or spectators (rule 3.18.4).

prompt: Can a protest still be heard after the award ceremony?
options: No, never
Yes: protests stay open for 24 hours
Only if the Head Official extends the period
Only if the Race Director agrees to hear it late
feedback: Protests go to the Head Official, who may extend a protest period beyond the award ceremony at their sole discretion (rule 3.19.3).

prompt: How must athletes come down from the Rope Climb?
options: Any way they like, once the bell has been rung
By dropping from the top, if the ground below is soft
Under control, with at least one hand on the rope
Down a different rope from the one they climbed up
feedback: At the Rope Climb, athletes must return to the ground in a safe and controlled manner, with at least one hand touching the rope at all times.

prompt: At a water crossing, an athlete dives in from the bank. What is the call?
options: Fine, if they stay inside the marked course
A failure: diving isn't allowed
A warning, as it's a safety matter
Fine, unless it gains them an advantage
feedback: Rule 4.3.9 says no diving at a swim or water crossing, and lists diving as a failure.

prompt: You think one of your obstacle's failure modes is too harsh for tired athletes. What do you do?
options: Apply it as written; escalate if unsure
Soften it as the day goes on
Use your own sense of what is fair
Apply it to Elite racers only
feedback: Judge against the obstacle's written failure modes, avoid judgement beyond the rule, and use the same interpretation from the first wave to the last. Escalate to the Head Referee when unsure.

prompt: An athlete asks to cut across a bend to avoid a slope you think is unsafe. What do you do?
options: Allow it: athlete safety always comes before the route
Allow it, if they take the penalty
Allow it, but record their headband number
Refuse, and report the hazard straight away
feedback: Athletes must cover the official course in its entirety (rule 3.6.1), so a shortcut is never yours to allow. Report the hazard straight away to the Head Referee, Race Director or Spartan staff.

prompt: Where there's no video, which decision does the officiating procedure make yours, on site?
options: Burpee number and quality, in writing
Whether a mandatory failure becomes a time penalty
The outcome of an athlete's protest
Which penalty format your obstacle uses
feedback: Without video, the referee decides burpee quantity and quality on site, writes it down and hands it to the Head Referee. The other decisions belong to the Race Director or the Head Referee.

prompt: At Olympus, an athlete rests a foot on one of the holds to get their breath. What is the call?
options: No failure: feet may rest on the wall
A failure: no feet on holds or holes
No failure, unless it gives an advantage
A failure only if they also touch the ground
feedback: Feet and knees may rest against the wall at Olympus, but touching any hold or hole with the feet is a failure (rule 4.2.10).

prompt: At the Monkey Bars, an athlete climbs the vertical truss like a ladder to reach the first bar. What is the call?
options: No failure: truss may be used to start the traverse
No failure, as the traverse hasn't begun
A failure: no vertical truss as a ladder
A failure only if they use it to finish
feedback: Rule 4.2.7 lists using vertical truss as a ladder as a failure, whether to start, traverse or finish. Only horizontal truss may be used to start or transfer.

prompt: Mid-traverse on the Monkey Bars, an athlete uses the horizontal truss to transfer. What is the call?
options: No failure: horizontal truss is allowed
A failure: any truss contact is banned on rigs
A failure: only the bars may be touched
No failure, but they restart that section
feedback: Rule 4.2.7 says horizontal truss may be used to start or transfer on the Monkey Bars. Vertical truss used as a ladder is the failure.

prompt: At the Helix, an athlete reaches across and uses a bar in the next lane. What is the call?
options: No failure, if the next lane is empty
A failure: only their own lane's bars
No failure, if it gives no advantage
A warning, then a failure next time
feedback: Rule 4.2.6 requires the Helix to be done using only the bars in a single lane. Using bars from another lane is a listed failure.

prompt: At the Multi-Rig, an athlete moves across into a second lane to reach a better attachment. What is the call?
options: A failure: it must stay in one lane
No failure, as they're using attachments only
No failure, if the other lane is free
A failure only if they also grab a chain
feedback: Rule 4.2.8 says the Multi-Rig is traversed using only the attachments, within one lane. Using more than one lane is a failure.

prompt: At which obstacles does the attempt start once four points of contact are made?
options: The Monkey Bars and the Multi-Rig
The Helix and the Z Wall
Olympus and the Monkey Bars
The Spear Throw and the Ape Hanger
feedback: The Helix and Z Wall attempts start at four points of contact (rules 4.2.6 and 4.2.17). At the Monkey Bars, Multi-Rig and Olympus it's once both feet leave the starting step.

prompt: On the 8 foot wall, an athlete pushes off the side of the wall to get over. What is the call?
options: No failure: only the straps are banned
A failure: no using the sides
No failure, as long as they get over
A failure only for male athletes
feedback: Rule 4.1.1 lists using the support structure, the sides of the wall or the straps as a failure on the 6 to 9 foot walls.

prompt: At the Z Wall, an athlete grips the top edge of a cutout for balance. What is the call?
options: No failure: cutouts are part of the wall to use
No failure, unless it gives an advantage
A failure: no touching a cutout's top or bottom
A failure only if a foot touches the ground
feedback: Rule 4.2.17 lists touching the top or bottom of any cutout as a Z Wall failure, alongside the ground, the top of the wall and the brace structures.
